artifact_schema.description: Two messages of equal length, both beginning with the pinned 64-byte prefix, as lowercase hex. The example's m is the prefix followed by one byte, so the prefix every submission has to carry is readable straight off this record.

m.description: The first message, lowercase hex, an even number of characters, at most 8192 of them.

m_prime.description: The second message, same length as m and different from it.

statement: Find a colliding pair for MD5 from a chaining value nobody chose. Both messages must begin with the same pinned 64-byte prefix -- exactly one message block for this function -- must have the same length, must differ somewhere, and must agree on the leading 48 of the 128 digest bits. The prefix is sha512("cairn hash-differential v1 md5-48"), so it is re-derivable by anyone and was chosen by nobody: a funder who picks a prefix can pick one whose chaining value they have already collided, and that is the self-dealing row in docs/threat-model.md. Deriving it also puts every published collision for MD5 out of reach as a copy, since all of them start from the standard IV behind a prefix their own author chose. Equal length is required because a same-length collision composes -- H(m || x) = H(m' || x) for every x -- and that is the property worth paying for. Messages are at most 4096 bytes and travel as lowercase hex in {"m", "m_prime"}. Only 48 bits have to agree, so a generic birthday search settles this in about 2^24 compressions with no cryptanalysis in it at all. It is a demonstration and not a bounty: the answer ships in examples/hash-differential/artifacts/md5-48.json, which is what makes the commit-reveal-audit loop runnable end to end and what shows this family of checkers accepts anything -- a checker shown only to reject is indistinguishable from one that rejects everything. Settling it a second time earns exactly zero.
